subject: math
intro: Hi, I'm Ms. Rivera. Dividing fractions is where a lot of 6th graders just memorize a trick — let's plan a lesson that builds meaning instead.

beats.narration: The title is the question students will keep asking themselves all period: how many fit?
This standard asks for interpreting and computing quotients of fractions — interpretation comes first.
I include "explain what the quotient means" because that's the part the trick skips.
beats.text: Students will be able to interpret and solve fraction division problems using visual models and explain what the quotient means in context.

beats.narration: I start with a whole number divided by a fraction because it's intuitive and gets everyone in.
beats.text: "You have 3 pizzas and each person eats 1/2 a pizza. How many people can you feed?" Students sketch it before we discuss.

beats.narration: Students discover the rule from the models, so it's their idea rather than a trick I handed them.
beats.text: Model 2 ÷ 1/3 and 3/4 ÷ 1/8 with fraction bars on the board, asking "How many 1/8s fit in 3/4?" each time. Only after three examples, look for a pattern with the class that leads to multiplying by the reciprocal.

beats.narration: Hands-on stations make the "how many fit" meaning concrete, especially for students who struggle with abstract symbols.
beats.text: Stations with ribbon, measuring cups, and fraction strips. Each station has a story problem; students model it physically, draw it, then write the equation.

beats.narration: Asking them to write the story checks meaning, not just computation.
beats.text: Write a story problem for 2 ÷ 1/4 and solve it with a drawing.

outro: Notice how every section keeps coming back to 'how many fit?' Now you plan one.
